topic: The Visual Heart of Linear Algebra: Vectors and Transformations
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students beginning Linear Algebra

sections.title: Vectors as Movements (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce vectors not as a list of numbers, but as arrows in a 2D coordinate system. Explain that every vector is a movement starting from the origin (0,0). Focus on the 'tip-to-tail' intuition and scaling (stretching/shrinking).
sections.example: A small ant named 'Vector' starts at the origin. To reach a crumb at (3, 2), he moves 3 units right and 2 units up. This arrow represents his displacement.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Basis Vectors (0:45-1:30)
sections.content: Introduce the unit basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Explain that any vector is just a 'linear combination'—a recipe of scaling these two fundamental building blocks. This sets the stage for understanding matrices.
sections.example: Imagine i-hat and j-hat are two magnetic tracks on the floor. To get to (3,2), the ant simply travels 3 times the length of i-hat and 2 times the length of j-hat.

sections.title: The Concept of Linear Transformation (1:30-2:30)
sections.content: Define a transformation as a function that takes an input vector and 'morphs' it into an output vector. Visually, this is shown as the entire coordinate grid warping. Crucially, emphasize that 'Linear' means grid lines remain parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays fixed.
sections.example: Imagine the 2D plane is a flexible rubber sheet with a grid drawn on it. A 'Transformation Device' grabs the corners and stretches it. If the grid lines remain straight and the center doesn't move, it's linear.

sections.title: Matrices as a Map of Basis Vectors (2:30-4:00)
sections.content: Show that a 2x2 matrix is simply a record of where i-hat and j-hat landed after the transformation. The first column is the new coordinate of i-hat; the second column is the new coordinate of j-hat. If you know where these two go, you know where every point on the grid goes.
sections.example: A 'Matrix Machine' takes a matrix [[0, -1], [1, 0]]. We watch i-hat move to (0,1) and j-hat move to (-1,0). The entire grid rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise. The matrix is just the 'GPS destination' for our basis vectors.

sections.title: The Determinant: Scaling Area (4:00-5:00)
sections.content: Explain the determinant geometrically. It is the factor by which areas are scaled during a transformation. If the determinant is 2, the area of any shape doubles. If it's 0, the space squishes into a line or a point (losing a dimension).
sections.example: A cat is sitting on a 1x1 square unit of the grid. After a transformation with a determinant of 3, the cat occupies 3 square units of space. If the determinant is 0, the cat is unfortunately flattened into a 1D line!
